messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM unbalanced group size
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vanesse,

Short answer: yes, it is already controlling for group *sizes*.  But it 
is not controlling for possible differences in group *sociality*, which 
one typically wants to do as well.

Long answer: because ERGMs are based on log odds, the group sizes 
implicitly end up in both the numerator and the denominator of all 
terms, and in that sense are controlled for.  So, if you have just a 
nodematch term, the null hypothesis against which the term is comparing 
is *not* that each group receives an equal absolute number of ties from 
each group; rather, each group receives ties in proportion to its group 
size from each group. In that sense, group size is controlled for.  But, 
often, different groups have overall different propensities for ties (in 
directed networks, this can break down into differences in sending 
and/or differences in receiving ties), regardless of who they are 
connecting to.  This is what nodefactor measures.  If you don't include 
nodefactor in your model, then different groups' propensities to have 
different amounts of ties overall will change the number of within-group 
ties away form the null described above, and appear as homophily when it 
really isn't.  So it is generally good to have a nodefactor term in 
there as well to disentangle this possible first-order (node-level) 
effect from the second-order (dyad-level) effect of homophily.

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vicki,

I think you are talking about two-paths, three-paths, and four-paths, 
right? Just to make sure we are talking about the same thing because a 
dyad and triad can usually be any permutation of edge configurations 
including two or three nodes, respectively.

In that case, you could apply a threshold value to the reachability 
matrix to retain only indirect paths of a certain length, sample dyads 
from the non-null entries of this matrix, and compute your test based on 
the two nodes' attributes.

You can compute the reachability matrix by using the "reachability" 
function from the sna package.

Best,
Philip

messages.body_plain:
Network Modeling for Epidemics
Summer short course at the University of Washington Aug 24-28, 2015

Network Modeling for Epidemics (NME) is a 5-day short course at the
University of Washington that provides an introduction to stochastic
network models for infectious disease transmission dynamics, with a focus
on empirically based modeling of HIV transmission.  It is a ?hands-on?
course, with the EpiModel software package (www.epimodel.org) that uses the
Statnet software suite in R, providing a unified framework for modeling
networks and epidemics.  Epimodel has a flexible open-source platform for
learning and building models. Resources include web-based tools, built-in
generic models that provide basic control over networks, pathogen
properties and demographics, and templates for user-programmed modules that
allow EpiModel to be extended to the full range of pathogens, hosts, and
disease dynamics.

The course uses mornings for lectures, and afternoons for labs with
students working in small groups.  On the final day, students have the
option of developing an EpiModel prototype for their own research projects,
with input from the instructors, which includes the lead EpiModel software
developer, Dr. Samuel Jenness.

Dates and location:
The course will be taught August 24-28 on the University of Washington
campus in Seattle.
Application dates and decision dates:
? April 15: Fellowship application deadline. Decisions will be made by
April 30.
? June 1:  General application deadline.  Applications will continue to be
accepted on a rolling basis until this date.  Decisions will be made by June
15.

Costs:
Course fee is $250. Travel and accommodation are the responsibility of the
participant, although discounted hotel rates are available, as are a
limited number of fellowships for pre-doctoral students or for attendees
from outside the US/Canada.

Application:
Apply online at https://catalyst.uw.edu/webq/survey/morrism/261658

Course website and more information:
http://bit.ly/NetworkEpi
http://epimodel.org

Returning students: For the first time this year, we encourage previous
attendees with active modeling projects to apply to return for a refresher
course. The EpiModel package has been significantly enhanced over the last
two years. Returning students with active projects will have the
opportunity to work closely with course instructors to address key
challenges in the design of their network model code.

Please free to share widely!

Yours,
Martina Morris, Steve Goodreau and Samuel Jenness

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Assuming the media are a passive node class (they don't create ties, only 
people can do that), this is neither a simple nor a bipartite network. 
Media are one mode with ties only to the other mode, while {students & 
teachers} are the other mode, for which all forms of within mode and 
between mode ties are allowed.  Courses form another "layer".  All in a 
dynamic setting where the evolution of different types of ties give rise 
to emergent positions.

That's a complicated process to model.

Since your events are instantaneous in continous time, you might want to 
look into Carter's relevent package.  ERGMs are designed for 
cross-sectional network analysis, and TERGMs are better suited to 
partnerships that have some kind of duration.

best,
Martina

That would be a standard ERGM.

ERGMs are generally used to represent the patterns of tie prevalence. 
TERGMS explicitly represent the process of tie formation and dissolution 
-- and the type of TERGM we have in statnet is a "separable" TERGM that 
uses an ERGM for each component.

Search for Pavel Krivitsky's papers -- they present the theory and 
methods.

mm

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Notice: Bug in latentnet's BIC calculation.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Users,

A bug has been discovered in latentnet versions prior to 2.7.0, in the
calculation of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). p + n(d+r+s)
was used as the number of parameters in the likelihood (where p is the
number of fixed effects, n the number of actors, d, the latent space
dimension, and r and s indicators of presence of sender and receiver (or
sociality) effects). This value should have been just p.

The following applications could have produced different results:
      * Using the BIC to select latent space dimension.
      * Using the BIC to decide whether or not to include random
        effects.

The following applications could not (i.e., would only be off by a
constant):
      * Using the BIC to select the number of clusters.
      * Using the BIC to select the fixed effects to be used.

We apologize for this error.

                                             Best Regards,
                                             Pavel Krivitsky

Hi, Fabiola -

On 03/27/2015 11:31 PM, Fabiola martinoli wrote:
> Dear Statnet's users and developers,
> i'm very new in ERGMs and i'm studying a network of 200 nodes for my 
> master's degree thesis. I have two questions for you:
>
> 1. How can i assess that my model converges properly? I mean, after i 
> receive my coefficients from the ergm() function, i check it with 
> mcmc.diagnostics(): the only important thing is that the MCMC sample 
> statistic are varying randomly around the observed values at each step 
> and that the difference between the observed and simulated values have 
> a roughly bell-shaped distribution centered in 0? Or should i also 
> check the individual p-values given at the end of the diagnostics?
> If so, what is the lower bound tha makes my p-value acceptable?
> I read a lot of papers and tutorial but i haven't found a clear answer 
> to my doubt.
>
As a practical matter, you want to verify that (1) the Markov chain is 
mixing well (e.g., you are covering the region of high probability with 
respect to each model statistic, the chain is not strongly 
autocorrelated, and the chain shows no signs of being "stuck" for long 
periods in a single state); (2) the mean of the sufficient statistics 
for the retained draws is close to their observed values; and 
(relatedly) (3) the Markov chain appears to be stationary (e.g., the 
first and second moments show no signs of "wandering").  The various 
diagnostics can assist with this process, although they can be 
over-interpreted.  (For instance, it is possible to obtain a perfectly 
reasonable parameter estimate from a sample that shows a significant 
departure of the simulated mean from (say) one of the observed 
statistics, and one can likewise obtain good results from a chain that 
is reasonably autocorrelated.  These are not good signs, however, and in 
practice one should work to minimize them.)

My own _practical_ advice for a typical case would be as follows:
   1. Verify that the first moment of the Markov chain has converged - 
the running mean line should be flat.  If there is evidence of a trend, 
either (1) the model is degenerate, and trying to head off to la-la 
land, or (2) you need to increase your burn-in time.
   2. Verify that the chain is mixing well.  You should see relatively 
smooth marginal distributions, there should be little visual evidence of 
strong autocorrelation in the trace plot, and autocorrelation 
diagnostics should show reasonably small correlations at reasonable 
lags.  If the chain isn't mixing well, either (1) your model is showing 
signs of being poorly behaved, or (2) you need to increase the thinning 
interval.
   3. Verify that the mean values of the sufficient statistics are 
reasonably close to the target values.  (Note that they may be a bit 
off, because if how the fitting algorithm works - we will provide a 
better test below.)  Ideally, the means will be within a standard 
deviation or so of the observed or target values.  If the means seem to 
be way off, this usually indicates insufficient burn-in and/or thinning 
length, but it can also result from a highly recalcitrant model with 
which the estimation algorithm cannot easily deal.
   4. Having done all of the above, produce a new, high-quality 
simulation from the fitted model (using simulate() or gof()). Verify 
(1)-(3) on the new sample; but this time, pay closer attention to (3).  
For a reasonable sample size (say, 250), I would usually be concerned if 
my mean statistics were significantly different from their target values 
(with the usual caveats about multiple testing and such).
   5. If your model clears all of the above, the fitting process itself 
has probably been successful.  You will still want to perform model 
adequacy checking and such, as described in the various available tutorials.

Again, these are heuristics, and one can identify exceptions and/or more 
specific directives for special cases.  But they should provide you with 
a good place to start.

> 2. I'm interested in studying a brokerage effect due to a nodal 
> attribute, is there any effect able to test it? I looked for it but i 
> can't find nothing.
>

This (and related!) problems are addressed in a forthcoming JSS paper:

Yaveroglu, Omer Nebil; Fitzhugh, Sean M.; Kurant, Maciej; Markopoulou, 
Athina; Butts, Carter T.; and Przulj, Natasa. (2015). ``ergm.graphlets: 
A Package for ERG Modeling Based on Graphlet Statistics.''  Journal of 
Statistical Software, forthcoming.

Unfortunately, it's been held up in the JSS editorial queue for months 
and months.  However, you can find a pre-print on arXiv: 
http://arxiv.org/abs/1405.7348.  Likewise, the package needed to add the 
associated statistics to ergm is on CRAN: 
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ergm.graphlets/index.html. Once 
you load the ergm.graphlets package, you can use the associated terms 
within ergm just as you would any other model terms.  (See the paper for 
examples.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Vanesse -

On 03/29/2015 08:03 AM, vanesse labeyrie wrote:
> Following these interesting precision, I have some additionnal questions concerning mcmc.diagnostics as I am concerned by the fairly subjective assessment of what is "reasonable"

Like virtually any statistical analysis conducted in a real world 
setting, expert judgment is an inescapable part of the ERGM model 
building, assessment, and interpretation process; anyone who tells you 
otherwise is trying to sell you something.  Just as there is no 
universally applicable rule for determining when the residuals in a 
regression are sufficiently well-behaved to permit the model to be 
trusted,* there is no simple and universal criterion for determining 
whether an ERGM MCMC is good enough for the model to be used - too much 
depends on the details of the situation, and the use to which the model 
will be put.  There are, however, a number of very effective heuristics 
that can and generally should be employed to assess convergence, fit, 
and adequacy.  As with other forms of statistical modeling, learning to 
use these heuristics effectively requires practice, and the component of 
expert judgment cannot be eliminated.

(*And, in any event, the residuals alone do not guarantee that the model 
has the properties that you want.)

> 1.could you precise what du you mean by "*autocorrelation diagnostics should show reasonably small correlations at reasonable lags*" ? what is a typical "small correlation" value ? (1 is not and 0 is, but in between ?)  and a reasonable lag ?
> as a non-expert it is difficult to know what is reasonable and what is not. I put one of my mcmc.diagnostics outputs at the end of the post as an example
>

The generality of my statement was not accidental: to determine whether 
your level of autocorrelation is problematic, you need to know something 
about the nature of the model, the sample size, etc. To learn more, I 
suggest taking a look at a good text on MCMC (I like the now old volume 
_Markov Chain Monte Carlo in Practice_, although there are many others) 
and looking at some of the results relating to autocorrelation, 
convergence, and effective sample size.  In the diagnostics returned by 
ergm(), you are going to want to assess whether your Markov chain's 
autocorrelation is reducing the effective sample size to the point where 
problems are arising. (This should happen less and less, because more 
and more automated checks for these sorts of issues are being 
implemented in ergm().) If you examine the detailed diagnostics, you 
should see for each statistic a "naive standard error" estimate and a 
"time series standard error" estimate - the former is based on an 
independent sample approximation, and the latter is corrected for serial 
autocorrelation.  To the extent that the latter is larger than the 
former, then serial autocorrelation in your sample (associated with e.g. 
slow mixing) is reducing the precision of calculations based on it.  (Of 
course, if both SEs are tiny, then this may be of no consequence: you 
need to compare them to the scale of reasonable variation in the 
associated statistic!  This is something that requires substantive 
knowledge, although the simulated standard deviation and the magnitude 
of the mean itself also provide useful clues.)   As far as the magnitude 
of the autocorrelation itself, you want it to be close to zero within a 
number of iterations that is small compared to your sample size.  There 
is no fixed value that is universally "small enough," but you can get a 
good sense of the impact of the degree of autocorrelation by studying 
the widely used "effective sample size" estimate of Neal: M = 
n/(1+2*sum_{k=1}^\infty rho_k), where M is the ESS, n is the total 
number of draws, and rho_k is the autocorrelation function at lag k.  If 
rho_k<<1 for k greater than some k', then M is going to be reduced (from 
n) by a factor of at most approximately 1+2*k'.  If n is big enough, you 
can tolerate a _lot_ of autocorrelation - but you are going to pay for 
it by having to run a very long Markov chain.  Likewise, the extent that 
you need a large ESS depends on how hard your model is to fit (which 
depends, among other things, on the roughness of exp(theta t(Y)) and the 
sharpness of the derivatives of the log normalizing factor in theta), 
and on how precise you need your estimates to be (which can depend e.g. 
on whether you are just trying to infer the signs of the elements of 
theta versus trying to simulate draws from a fitted model).  These 
tradeoffs are application-specific, and can in some cases require one to 
study one's problem at considerable length.

To turn to the case you showed, it looks to me like you have enough 
autocorrelation that its effects are noticeable (e.g., in the corrected 
SEs of the mean stats).  OTOH, the time series SEs are still a few 
orders of magnitude smaller than the variation around the mean stats, so 
this may not be a problem; given that your trace plots are OK in that 
specific respect, I wouldn't worry about it. I'm more concerned about 
the fact that the trace plots suggest that your mean stats 
systematically depart from the observed values. That and the Geweke 
diagnostic suggest that you haven't burned the model in sufficiently - 
given how slowly it's mixing, you might need a lot more iterations, or 
else you might need to inspect the model and see if one of the terms 
(e.g., one of the curved terms) is poorly calibrated.  (Using gwesp and 
gdsp in the same model can also cause problems.)  However, a better way 
to assess whether the mean stats have really converged is to simulate 
draws from the fitted model, and examine them in that context.  (You are 
really looking at the model that was one iteration removed from the 
final fitted model.)  If the mean model statistics from the fitted model 
closely match the target statistics, then absent other problems I would 
not be inclined to worry overmuch about the above.  If, OTOH, you see 
the same problems in the new simulation, then you probably need to 
return to the fitting process.

> 2.  when saying that "t*he mean values of the sufficient statistics are reasonably close to the target values*" this is also fairly subjective - For instance, what shall I conclude from my example mcmcm.diagnostics output plots attached to this post ?
> For instance, the gwdegree is the term which shows the most important departure from observed, but when assessing GOF, the plots and p-values are not bad (see attached file gof).
> Tutorial moslty provide fairly extreme examples of non-convergence, but I find it difficult to asses convergence quality when situations are less contrasted.
>

See above.  What constitutes "close enough" in an ambiguous case is 
going to depend on how bad the model's problems seem to be, whether 
those problems seem to impact the features about which you care, and the 
level of precision you need in your answer.  While there are cases that 
are obviously and pretty universally pathological, and cases that are 
obviously and near-universally well-behaved, many real-world models lie 
somewhere between.  In those cases, there is no escaping the exercise of 
judgment, informed by knowledge of the system under study and the 
problem one is trying to solve.  That doesn't mean that "anything goes" 
- decisions made during the modeling process should be defensible, and 
guided by principle - but there is unlikely to be a single, uniform 
protocol that one can automatically follow and that solves all problems.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

>>     Dear Statnet's users and developers,
>>     i'm very new in ERGMs and i'm studying a network of 200 nodes for
>>     my master's degree thesis. I have two questions for you:
>>
>>     1. How can i assess that my model converges properly? I mean,
>>     after i receive my coefficients from the ergm() function, i check
>>     it with mcmc.diagnostics(): the only important thing is that the
>>     MCMC sample statistic are varying randomly around the observed
>>     values at each step and that the difference between the observed
>>     and simulated values have a roughly bell-shaped distribution
>>     centered in 0? Or should i also check the individual p-values
>>     given at the end of the diagnostics?
>>     If so, what is the lower bound tha makes my p-value acceptable?
>>     I read a lot of papers and tutorial but i haven't found a clear
>>     answer to my doubt.

>     As a practical matter, you want to verify that (1) the Markov
>     chain is mixing well (e.g., you are covering the region of high
>     probability with respect to each model statistic, the chain is not
>     strongly autocorrelated, and the chain shows no signs of being
>     "stuck" for long periods in a single state); (2) the mean of the
>     sufficient statistics for the retained draws is close to their
>     observed values; and (relatedly) (3) the Markov chain appears to
>     be stationary (e.g., the first and second moments show no signs of
>     "wandering"). The various diagnostics can assist with this
>     process, although they can be over-interpreted.  (For instance, it
>     is possible to obtain a perfectly reasonable parameter estimate
>     from a sample that shows a significant departure of the simulated
>     mean from (say) one of the observed statistics, and one can
>     likewise obtain good results from a chain that is reasonably
>     autocorrelated.  These are not good signs, however, and in
>     practice one should work to minimize them.)
>
>     My own _practical_ advice for a typical case would be as follows:
>       1. Verify that the first moment of the Markov chain has
>     converged - the running mean line should be flat. If there is
>     evidence of a trend, either (1) the model is degenerate, and
>     trying to head off to la-la land, or (2) you need to increase your
>     burn-in time.
>       2. Verify that the chain is mixing well.  You should see
>     relatively smooth marginal distributions, there should be little
>     visual evidence of strong autocorrelation in the trace plot, and
>     autocorrelation diagnostics should show reasonably small
>     correlations at reasonable lags.  If the chain isn't mixing well,
>     either (1) your model is showing signs of being poorly behaved, or
>     (2) you need to increase the thinning interval.
>       3. Verify that the mean values of the sufficient statistics are
>     reasonably close to the target values. (Note that they may be a
>     bit off, because if how the fitting algorithm works - we will
>     provide a better test below.)  Ideally, the means will be within a
>     standard deviation or so of the observed or target values.  If the
>     means seem to be way off, this usually indicates insufficient
>     burn-in and/or thinning length, but it can also result from a
>     highly recalcitrant model with which the estimation algorithm
>     cannot easily deal.
>       4. Having done all of the above, produce a new, high-quality
>     simulation from the fitted model (using simulate() or gof()). 
>     Verify (1)-(3) on the new sample; but this time, pay closer
>     attention to (3).  For a reasonable sample size (say, 250), I
>     would usually be concerned if my mean statistics were
>     significantly different from their target values (with the usual
>     caveats about multiple testing and such).
>       5. If your model clears all of the above, the fitting process
>     itself has probably been successful.  You will still want to
>     perform model adequacy checking and such, as described in the
>     various available tutorials.
>
>     Again, these are heuristics, and one can identify exceptions
>     and/or more specific directives for special cases.  But they
>     should provide you with a good place to start.
